page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The rule
lines: Hund's rule: in degenerate orbitals, pairing
of electrons begins only after every
degenerate orbital has one electron each.
The unpaired electrons have parallel spins.
steps.why: Degenerate orbitals have equal energy. Two electrons in one orbital repel each other, so the lower-energy arrangement puts one electron in each orbital first.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the word degenerate. The rule applies only to orbitals of equal energy.
Forgetting to say the single electrons have parallel spins.
steps.memory_tip: Every degenerate orbital takes one electron before any of them takes a second.
steps.margin_note: The words degenerate and pairing must both appear.

steps.label: The example
lines: None of the three 2p orbitals holds a pair.
steps.why: Nitrogen is the standard example because its three 2p electrons exactly fill the three degenerate 2p orbitals one each, so the rule is visible in a single configuration.
common_mistakes: Writing 2p³ as one orbital holding a pair and one holding a single electron.
steps.memory_tip: Nitrogen has exactly three 2p electrons for exactly three 2p orbitals. One each, no pairs.
steps.margin_note: Drawing the three boxes with single upward arrows is accepted here.

insider_note: The rule alone is half the answer. The examiner expects a worked example, and nitrogen is the one every textbook uses.
